common_name: Ralls Janet Apple (Late-Season Virginia Heirloom, Parent of Red Delicious and Fuji)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in early spring while still dormant, in well-drained soil away from late-spring frost pockets.

directions: Ralls Janet dates to 18th-century Virginia and became famous in 20th-century Missouri and Illinois orchards for its ability to shrug off harsh winters and heat waves alike. Very late bloom time helps the flowers dodge spring frosts that damage earlier-flowering apples, and the small, firm, tart-sweet fruit stores in a root cellar into late winter. It is one of the two parents of Red Delicious and, through a Japanese breeding program, a grandparent of Fuji, making it an interesting living link for gardeners who grow both modern and heirloom apples. Choose it for its toughness and storability rather than fresh-eating size, since the fruit is on the small side compared to modern dessert apples.

common_name: Early Harvest Apple (Classic Early-Season American Heirloom)

planting.note: Plant in early spring in full sun and well-drained soil, siting the tree where late-summer fruit can be checked every few days as it ripens unevenly.

directions: One of the oldest named apples grown in American gardens, Early Harvest was prized in colonial and 19th-century orchards for ripening well before almost any other cultivar, often in midsummer. The pale yellow-green skin and tender, tart flesh cook down quickly into sauce and are best picked and used within days, since the fruit bruises easily and does not store. Because the whole crop does not ripen at once, expect several light pickings over a couple of weeks rather than one harvest. Grow it as a nostalgia piece or for the earliest homemade applesauce of the season, not as a keeper apple.

common_name: York Imperial Apple (Pennsylvania Heirloom Keeping and Cider Apple)

planting.note: Plant a compatible pollinizer nearby, since York Imperial is not reliably self-fertile and blooms mid-season.

directions: Discovered near York, Pennsylvania in the early 1800s, this apple built the Mid-Atlantic processing and cider industry for over a century thanks to its exceptional storage life and steady yields. The fruit has a distinctive lopsided, flattened shape and firm yellow flesh with a red blush, making it easy to pick out among other apples in the bin. Flavor is mild and sweet-tart, better suited to pies, cider blends, and long winter storage than fresh eating off the tree. Choose York Imperial where a long-keeping, reliable dual-purpose apple with real regional history matters more than dessert-apple looks.

common_name: Golden Russet Apple (American Heirloom Dessert and Cider Russet)
subcategory: high-sugar heirloom russet apple for fresh eating and cider

planting.note: Plant in full sun with good air circulation to keep the thin russeted skin dry and reduce scab pressure.

directions: This 19th-century American heirloom is distinct from the English russets already common in orchards, carrying some of the highest natural sugar content of any apple, which cidermakers prize for producing high-alcohol, well-balanced ferments. The small to medium fruit has a rough golden-bronze skin over crisp, honeyed flesh that is equally good eaten fresh once fully ripe in fall. The tree tends toward biennial bearing and benefits from thinning in a heavy year to even out production. Plant it for a dual-purpose tree that serves both the cider press and the fresh fruit bowl.

common_name: Harrison Apple (Historic Newark New Jersey Cider Apple)

planting.note: Plant in full sun on well-drained soil; the vigorous, disease-resistant tree tolerates light neglect once established.

directions: Harrison built the reputation of the once-famous Newark cider of colonial and early Federal-era New Jersey, prized for its deep color and high alcohol content pressed from a single variety rather than a blend. The small, dry-textured, black-speckled yellow fruit is far too astringent and mealy for fresh eating but yields juice with excellent sugar and tannin balance. Nearly lost to cultivation, it was rediscovered in an old New Jersey orchard in the 1970s and has since been preserved by heritage cider growers. Choose it specifically for serious home cidermaking, not for a dessert or baking apple.
sources: Rutgers New Jersey Agricultural Experiment Station

common_name: Hewes Virginia Crab Apple (Colonial-Era Cider Crabapple)

planting.note: Plant in full sun; the tough, disease-tolerant tree needs little pampering once its roots are established.

directions: Grown at Monticello and documented by Thomas Jefferson himself, this small, hard, tannic crabapple was a workhorse of colonial Virginia cider production, adding astringency and complexity when blended with sweeter apples at the press. The tree is markedly tougher and more disease-resistant than standard dessert apples, tolerating poorer soil and less spray attention. Fruit is far too tannic and small to eat out of hand, so it is grown specifically as a blending variety for traditional heritage ciders. Choose it to recreate historically accurate colonial-style cider or to add backbone to a home cider blend.

subcategory: extremely cold-hardy Upper Midwest heirloom apple

planting.note: Plant a compatible pollinizer within range, since Haralson blooms mid-season and needs cross-pollination to fruit well.

directions: Released by the University of Minnesota in 1922, Haralson was bred specifically to survive winters that kill most other apple trees and became the most widely planted apple in Minnesota for much of the 20th century. The medium, deep-red fruit is firm and notably tart, holding its shape well in pies and sauce, with flavor that mellows somewhat in storage. Its extreme cold hardiness makes it a reliable choice where winter low temperatures rule out many popular commercial cultivars. Plant it in northern gardens as a dependable, disease-tolerant workhorse rather than for dessert-apple sweetness.

planting.note: Plant in full sun with a pollinizer nearby, and pick promptly once ripe since fruit does not hold long in storage.

directions: Released by the University of Minnesota in 1999 out of the same breeding program that later produced Honeycrisp, Zestar! ripens in late summer, weeks ahead of most main-season apples, filling a gap for gardeners wanting a crisp fresh apple early in the season. The flavor pairs bright tartness with a distinctive brown-sugar sweetness and a notably crunchy texture for such an early apple. Winter hardiness is excellent, letting it succeed in cold northern gardens where many early apples struggle. Grow it for the first crisp, flavorful apple of the year, but plan to eat or process the crop quickly since it does not store as long as later-season cultivars.
